title: The unforgiving servant
hookLine: a man forgiven a huge debt throttles someone over a small one (Matthew 18:23–35)

lines: BE PATIENT, I'LL PAY IT ALL.
cards: A king sits down to go through his accounts, and one servant is brought in owing him ten thousand talents. The text says plainly he has nothing to pay it with.
The king orders him sold, with his wife and children and everything he has. The servant falls down before him and begs: be patient, I'll pay it all.
And the king, moved with compassion, lets him go and forgives the whole debt. The servant walks out a free man. What he does next is the whole story.

teach.h: BY THE THROAT, OVER A SMALL DEBT.
teach.b: First, the turn. Outside, the forgiven servant runs into a fellow servant who owes him an hundred pence, in the King James words. A small sum beside an impossible one.

He "laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest." The fellow servant falls down and begs with almost the same words: "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all."
The same plea that just saved the first man. He refuses, and has him thrown in prison until he pays. Second, the witnesses.
The other servants see it, are very sorry, and tell the king everything. Mercy, and the lack of it, gets noticed. Third, the question at the center.

teach.h: EVEN AS I HAD PITY ON THEE.
teach.b: The king calls the man back and asks: "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?" That's the whole parable in one line. His problem isn't that he wanted his money.
He walked out of the biggest mercy of his life and let it change nothing about how he treated anyone else.

teach.h: A HARD ENDING, READ TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Fourth, the hard ending. The king hands him over to the tormentors, and Jesus closes with a warning about forgiving a brother from the heart. Christians read that ending differently.

teach.h: SHOULDEST NOT THOU ALSO HAVE HAD COMPASSION?
teach.b: Some take it as a stark warning about judgment. Others hear a picture of what an unforgiving heart already does to itself: it locks itself in. Both readings keep the same center.
The man forgot he had been forgiven.

how: Christians read the parable of the unforgiving servant as part of Jesus's answer to Peter about forgiveness, since Matthew places it right after seventy times seven.

"have patience with me, and I will pay thee all": the plea that had just saved the first man.

games.q: you've just been forgiven a debt you could never pay. outside, you meet someone who owes you a small sum. what does the servant in the story do?
o: seizes him by the throat and demands payment.
gives him more time to pay.
games.why: he "took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest," and threw him in prison. the other servants saw it all.

practice: Remember a time someone let you off: a parent who didn't stay angry, a friend who took you back, a stranger who was kind when you'd been rude.
Stay with what they chose not to collect, then let someone come to mind who owes you something small, and hold the two side by side, the way the story does.
If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the mercy you received.
